title: Special and Hyperspecial Points in the Bruhat-Tits Building
body_html:
Special and Hyperspecial Points in the Bruhat-Tits Building

Among all points (or vertices) in the Bruhat-Tits building \(\mathcal{B}(G, F)\), those with the richest arithmetic structure — a reductive group scheme model over the valuation ring — are the hyperspecial points. More generally, special and superspecial points have partial or enhanced versions of this property.

Setup

Let \(G\) be a connected reductive group over a non-archimedean local field \(F\) with valuation ring \(\mathcal{O}_F\), residue field \(\mathbb{F}_q\), and Bruhat-Tits building \(\mathcal{B}(G, F)\).

Fix a maximal \(F\)-split torus \(S \subseteq G\), giving an apartment \(\mathcal{A}(S, F)\). The affine root system \(\Psi\) of \(G\) relative to \(S\) acts on \(\mathcal{A}\) by affine reflections, partitioning the apartment into alcoves (open chambers).

Special vertices

A vertex \(x \in \mathcal{B}(G, F)\) is special (Kaletha-Prasad §7.11) if every wall of \(\mathcal{A}\) is parallel to some wall passing through \(x\). More precisely:

Definition. A point \(x \in \mathcal{A}(S, F)\) is absolutely special if for every affine root \(\psi \in \Psi\) (i.e.\ every affine hyperplane), there exists an affine root \(\psi' \in \Psi\) parallel to \(\psi\) that passes through \(x\).

Equivalently, \(x\) is special iff the local Weyl group at \(x\) (the subgroup of the affine Weyl group \(W_{\mathrm{aff}}\) fixing \(x\)) is isomorphic to the full finite Weyl group \(W_0\).

In the absolute building \(\mathcal{B}(G_K, K)\) (for a splitting field \(K/F\)), a vertex is \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-special if it is fixed by \(\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)\) and is special in \(\mathcal{B}(G_K, K)\).

Hyperspecial points

Definition. A point \(x \in \mathcal{B}(G, F)\) is hyperspecial if the parahoric group scheme \(G_x^0 \to \operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_F)\) is a reductive group scheme — i.e.\ the special fiber \((G_x^0)_{\mathbb{F}_q}\) is a connected reductive algebraic group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) (with trivial unipotent radical).

Equivalently, \(x\) is hyperspecial iff the natural filtration \(G(F)_{x,0} \supset G(F)_{x,0^+}\) satisfies \[ G(F)_{x,0} / G(F)_{x,0^+} \;\cong\; G_{\mathbb{F}_q}(\mathbb{F}_q), \] where \(G_{\mathbb{F}_q}\) is a connected reductive group over \(\mathbb{F}_q\).

Superspecial points

A vertex \(x\) in the building of an absolutely almost simple group \(G\) is superspecial (Kaletha-Prasad §9.9, §10.2) if \(x\) is hyperspecial and, additionally, \(x\) is fixed by all automorphisms of the building. Superspecial points are the "most symmetric" vertices and exist only in special cases.

Characterization: when do hyperspecial points exist?

Theorem (Tits, Kaletha-Prasad §9.9). Hyperspecial points in \(\mathcal{B}(G, F)\) exist if and only if \(G\) is unramified: quasi-split over \(F\) and split over a maximal unramified extension \(F^{\mathrm{unr}}/F\).

When \(G\) is unramified: - Hyperspecial vertices exist and form a single \(G(F)\)-orbit. - The parahoric group scheme at a hyperspecial vertex is a reductive model \(\mathbf{G} / \mathcal{O}_F\) with \(\mathbf{G}_{F} = G\), unique up to isomorphism; it is the Chevalley group scheme for the split form, twisted by the Frobenius.

When \(G\) is ramified (but quasi-split), special vertices still exist but their special fibers have non-trivial unipotent radicals.

The reductive quotient at a special vertex

At a special vertex \(x\): - The special fiber \((G_x^0)_{\mathbb{F}_q}\) is connected. - If \(x\) is hyperspecial, this special fiber is reductive with the same root system as \(G\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). - For non-hyperspecial special \(x\): the reductive quotient has a root system that is a proper subsystem of the absolute root system of \(G\).

Examples

\(\mathrm{SL}_2(F)\) split

The building is a regular tree of valency \(q+1\). There are two conjugacy classes of vertices: - Class 1: stabilizer \(\cong \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathcal{O}_F)\), reductive special fiber \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{F}_q)\) — hyperspecial. - Class 2 (for the other conjugacy class): stabilizer is a conjugate of the above; also hyperspecial.

(For \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) all vertices are hyperspecial, since \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) is split.)

\(\mathrm{SL}_2\) over a ramified quadratic extension \(E/F\) (viewed as a non-split group)

For the group \(U_3\) (a quasi-split but ramified unitary group), there are no hyperspecial vertices; all special vertices have a parahoric group scheme whose special fiber is an extension of a reductive group by a unipotent group.

\(\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\)

All vertices in the building of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) are hyperspecial (since \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) is split). They correspond to \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}_F)\)-conjugates, i.e.\ to \(\mathcal{O}_F\)-lattices \(L \subseteq F^n\) up to homothety; the associated parahoric group scheme is \(\mathrm{GL}(L/\mathcal{O}_F)\).

Role in the Langlands program

  • Satake isomorphism. The spherical Hecke algebra at a hyperspecial vertex \(K = G(\mathcal{O}_F)\) is \(\mathcal{H}(G(F), K) \cong \mathbb{C}[X_*(T)]^{W_0}\), the complexified representation ring of the Langlands dual group \(\hat{G}\).
  • Unramified representations. A smooth irreducible representation of \(G(F)\) with a \(K\)-fixed vector (for \(K\) hyperspecial) is unramified; these are in bijection with semisimple conjugacy classes in \(\hat{G}\) (Satake correspondence / spherical Langlands).
  • Good reduction. A geometric object (abelian variety, automorphic Galois representation) has good reduction at a prime \(v\) of a global field iff the associated local group has a hyperspecial model at \(v\).
